teaching_card.title: Usage and Idioms (Medium)
teaching_card.body: ACT English tests whether you use the right word, not just a grammatical one. Commonly confused pairs (affect/effect, than/then, fewer/less, lie/lay), fixed prepositions (different from, capable of), comparatives versus superlatives, and precise, non-redundant wording all show up here. Read for meaning first, then match the word to the job it must do.
key_points: Decide the part of speech the blank needs, then pick the word that fits it.
Count the things compared: two take -er/more, three or more take -est/most.
Learn idioms as pairs: different from, capable of, interested in, prefer X to Y.
Cut words that repeat an idea already stated ('reopen again', 'final and last').
teaching_card.worked_example: 'The frost did not ___ the harvest.' A verb is needed, so 'affect' (to influence), not the noun 'effect'.

screens.title: Confusable pairs
screens.body: Many wrong answers are real words in the wrong job. 'Affect' is usually the verb, 'effect' the noun. 'Than' compares; 'then' orders events in time. 'Fewer' counts things; 'less' measures amounts. 'Lie' means to recline (lie, lay, lain); 'lay' means to place something (lay, laid, laid) and always takes an object.
key_points: fewer for countable nouns; less for amounts.
lay needs an object; lie does not.

screens.title: Idioms and prepositions
screens.body: Some words are glued to a particular preposition: different FROM, capable OF, interested IN, consistent WITH, prefer X TO Y, based ON. There is no rule to derive these; when a choice swaps the preposition, say the phrase aloud and trust the standard pairing.

screens.title: Comparing two vs. three or more
screens.body: Use the comparative (-er or 'more') when exactly two things are compared and the superlative (-est or 'most') for three or more. Never stack markers: 'more shorter' and 'most tallest' are always wrong.
key_points: Of the two routes, the coastal one is SHORTER.
Of the three routes, the coastal one is the SHORTEST.

screens.title: Precise, not padded
screens.body: Choose the word that says exactly what is meant in the sentence's register: a study 'demonstrates', a dispute is 'resolved', seedlings are 'planted'. Then strip redundancy: 'reopen again', 'mutually agreed together', and 'final and last' each say one thing twice.
screens.worked_example: The museum will reopen (not 'reopen again') its east wing in May.
